EntertainmentTab.title: ‘One person turned up at my house’: Russell T Davies on fierce fandom, finding love after grief - and the fear that drives him to keep a knife by the door
EntertainmentTab.text:
Russell T Davies is a man who prefers to look on the bright side. That time he was gay-bashed by a gang of bus conductors? “People have been beaten up far worse than me, that was just a bit of a thumping in the street.” When the production schedule of his dystopian drama Years and Years forced him back to work within days of his husband’s death? “Writing was a nice escape.” Even a story about his “tough” father branding him “yesterday’s man” after his initial departure as showrunner on Doctor Who concludes with a cheerful: “I knew I wasn’t.” It’s easy to see how he’s earned a reputation as the most affable man in TV, if not the world. So why has he taken to keeping a kitchen knife by his front door, “ready to use”?

“I’m called a paedophile and a groomer online by people like [Father Ted creator and anti-trans activist] Graham Linehan, and now people believe what they read. People believe it when they’re told the Earth is flat,” he says. His support for trans rights has resulted in years of death threats and “groomer” smears, which he used to brush off. “But the online world is becoming the real world. People have worked out my address, and one person turned up at my house. If you believe a paedophile lives here, it’s not the maddest thing in the world to come and get me. I’ve been saying for years that our rights are paper-thin, and here we are. What scares me is that I can’t see an end to it. Nothing is going to unseat these tech barons – it will require some sort of revolution to stop them. So for the first time in history, hatred is being monetised by an algorithm.”

Davies, 63, is the great chronicler of queer British life, having made his name with the groundbreaking (and jaw-dropping) Queer As Folk in 1999. The show followed the lives of three gay men in Manchester, and was a surprise hit, but not without its provocations. The Daily Mail wrote that, “Any nation which allows this … [is] hell-bent on destruction.” Among the controversies was its depiction of a one-night stand between Stuart, 29, and Nathan, 15. In today’s climate, where accusations of grooming are regularly levelled at gay men, would he still write such an inflammatory storyline? “I would,” he says. “Although it’s slightly different these days – because in 1999 Nathan would’ve been in school under section 28 [a law banning the ‘promotion’ of homosexuality], meaning that he had no one to talk to. I was trying to say, ‘This is what’s going to happen.’ Of course, Nathan wants to get fucked, and he’s got no one to talk to about it. People say: ‘Oh my God, he was 15, that’s illegal.’ It’s a drama!”

We’re meeting to discuss The Queerest of Folk, a galloping memoir of Davies’s life as Britain’s most celebrated showrunner. He’s previously criticised the new generation of TV writers for prioritising positive representation over good storytelling – his own interest lies in the nuances. His most recent drama, Tip Toe, about a simmering feud between neighbours on opposite ends of the political divide that boils into a horrific act of violence, upset some viewers by including a gender-critical character, Stephanie. What inspired her? “I think it’s important to hear all voices. Years and Years and It’s a Sin both had lead gay characters who were Tory voters – if you watch most dramas you’d think those people don’t exist. I know people who are gender critical. The whole argument is so polarised that to some people the fact that she’s gender critical means she might as well be a murderer, which is just nonsense. There are people with genuine concerns, and they need to be discussed. Where is the debate?”

Another character, Melba, delivers a powerful monologue about the state of LGBTQ+ rights, with a fleeting reference to ‘‘women who are furious, and with good reason”. What did he mean? “He’s saying maybe on the issue of women’s sports he agrees [with a gender-critical perspective]. We left it vague, but why’s there an assumption that no camp gay man would ever say that? Why’s it a surprise? I could absolutely go out on Canal Street and find you a rightwing drag queen. It’s important to show that. It’s kind of my job to show those complexities.”

Davies is a titan of television – and in real life. His 6ft 6in frame fills the doorway of his Swansea home, where he greets me with literal open arms. Inside, I’m gratified to discover that the TV is on; he famously never turns it off, even when he goes out (“My new one turns itself off automatically. I really resent that.”). It continues humming away in the living room while we chat at his dining room table, which features a ceramic Tardis and is overlooked by an original Peanuts cartoon illustration – a rare splurge that cost him £2,000. His parents, both classics teachers, were the same, leaving the TV on even when they had guests.

Despite their “awe” at television, Davies could never quite bring himself to admit to his father that he wrote for it full-time. “My mum said never to tell him that I didn’t have a normal nine-to-five job, because he would just nag me about it, he’d never understand. So until his death he never knew.” In 1991, when Davies quit his job as a children’s TV producer to pursue writing, he omitted to tell his dad, Vivian. “When I’d have dramas on television that I’d written, he’d ask: ‘When did you do that, then?’ And I’d say: ‘In my spare time.’” Vivian was blind for the last 25 years of his life, which could make him quite “angry and result in moments of nastiness which didn’t become him” (hence the “yesterday’s man” comment). One consequence of his blindness was that Davies’s mum had to narrate the action of Queer As Folk to him. Davies prefers not to dwell on this. “Can you imagine her having to describe rimming? I think I gave it to them on Christmas Eve.”

His first memory is at three and a half watching the original Doctor Who, William Hartnell, regenerate. “Someone told me the other day that you don’t have strong memories before the age of six, but that’s not true. That episode is missing from the BBC archives, but it’s burned into my head.” It was an origin story in more ways than one; his biggest triumph came when he successfully lobbied the BBC to relaunch Doctor Who after a 16-year hiatus (today, I notice that even his shower is home to a toy Dalek). During his initial tenure as showrunner, from 2005 to 2010, it became the No 1 show on British television. In June 2009, he decided to leave on a high, moving to Los Angeles where he was commissioned to write Cucumber (about a middle-aged man confronting his gay shame) for Showtime, but declined roles rewriting Skyfall and working on a George Lucas Star Wars project. He later turned down another role writing on a little show called Succession.

Then in 2011, Davies’s partner of 12 years, Andrew Smith, started having “hallucinations of an Edwardian lady smiling at him sarcastically”. These turned out to be symptoms of a stage four brain tumour, and Smith was initially given just 18 months to live. In a 2007 interview, Davies had said his focus was on his work adding: “If I’m writing, I would walk over [Andrew’s] body if he had a heart attack.” But when Smith fell ill, the opposite turned out to be true. The pair moved back to the UK, and Davies quit work to become Smith’s carer. “I surprised myself. Before that, I’d have thought I wouldn’t be able to do it; I’d hire nurses and get people in and outsource it. But when it comes to it, you realise you don’t want a stranger looking after him.”

Despite his initial prognosis, Smith lived until 2018. Davies resumed working from their home in Manchester – relocating Cucumber from Seattle to Canal Street and winning best writer at the Bafta Cymru awards for A Very English Scandal, among other projects – but rarely left Smith’s side. “We were together for 20 years, but when I think of him now, I think of the last eight years,” he says, his Welsh boom softening. “Up until that time, we’d never really lived together. From 2011 onwards, the memories are vivid. I remember every day, almost. It’s weird, because there’s intimacy in a life-or-death situation. There was honesty. He lived much longer than expected, and so every year after that became a joy.” After his death, Davies writes that he spent eight years sitting at home. In practice, this meant completing Years and Years, a surprise return as showrunner on Doctor Who, and writing the Royal Television Society award-winning It’s a Sin (about the Aids crisis), the Helena Bonham Carter-starring biographical miniseries Nolly (about another of his early obsessions, the Crossroads star Noele Gordon) and Tip Toe, alongside other ventures. Aside from these professional highs, Davies concedes that, “It was a little bit monastic.” Then, once again, his optimism rallies. “But I’m happy watching the telly. It was quiet, but that was fine.”

Last year, this relative quiet was broken when Davies met Oliver Cole, a 27-year-old model on Instagram. “I normally ignore DMs, but I looked at his photos and thought, ‘Oh, hello!’” he hoots. “We DMd each other for about three months. Not sexting. I didn’t think it was anything like that, because of his age. But he was such a nice man that I thought I’d have dinner with him. It turned out it was far more than that. He’s lovely.” Cole has since become Davies’s third ever boyfriend. “Isn’t that mad?”

I’m curious to know how Davies’s friends reacted to their 36-year age difference. “They were all very polite. I’m absolutely certain behind my back some of them were saying: ‘What the hell?’ But then they met him. He’s quite extraordinary. He’s Australian, and they tend to be quite tough and ahead of the game and know what they think. I was dreading what [Davies’s long-term producer] Nicola Shindler might think. Then she met him and said: ‘Oh! I get it, he’s lovely.’” Did Smith encourage Davies to meet someone else after his death? “He’d be really happy. His doctor was at another hospital when the final scan results came in saying he was going to die. She phoned me and said: ‘I can come to the hospital tomorrow and tell him, or you can.’ Actually, I was honoured to tell him. I thought it was better coming from me than anyone else. And this describes how lovely he was – when I told him, the first thing he said was: ‘I feel sorry for you.’ I found that extraordinary. Nobody knew me better than Andrew, and I think he’d be sad to think of me on my own.”

Davies divides his time between houses in Manchester and Swansea, replicas of each other, with the same crockery and Pantone colour mugs (today’s choice is yellow). He’s “saved like a miser”, since the early 90s, when he was told it was impossible for writers to make money. This nest egg allowed him to care for Smith during the years when he didn’t work, but even today he struggles to spend. “I’m still miserly. If I like a shirt that costs £20, a voice says: ‘Can I afford that?’ I get paid a nice wage, but I’ll see something online I like for £30 and think: ‘That’s too much!’” In the late 90s, he went out on Canal Street every night of the week – he met Smith in Cruz 101 nightclub 10 minutes before closing – but these days he’s happiest writing, or in front of the TV, and has a dread of parties. Kate Bush invited him for dinner during his first stint on Doctor Who, but he’s yet to fix a date.

In January, Cole persuaded Davies to take his first holiday in 14 years, to New York. “It was lovely,” he smiles. “Although I’m not a natural traveller, I can’t bear airports, they’re horrible.” Last November, Cole posted a video of himself in the Tardis. Is he a Doctor Who fan? “He is, but that takes about five minutes of conversation; it’s not like we sit there discussing [show antagonist] the Rani. When it became a relationship, I reported it to the bosses at Doctor Who, in case anyone tried to say I was abusing my position by going out with a fan.” At its height, the show was drawing a record 13 million viewers, which I suggest represents quite a wide dating pool of fans. “And there’s not many you’d go out with,” he laughs. “You know that’s true!”

If Davies is ribbingly dismissive of some of the show’s more rabid fandom, then the feeling has become mutual. Twenty-one years after he rocketed Doctor Who to unprecedented heights, his most recent time as showrunner was polarising, with some fans criticising convoluted story arcs and anti-climactic plot resolutions. In June, his exit left the show at a perilous juncture. A Disney+ partnership with the BBC ended after two seasons of disappointing ratings, and the show is now off air while production of future series is put out to competitive tender.

Was he wounded by the reaction? “I’m not personally wounded by that,” he says. “I thought it was a shame. And maybe I wonder if I should have done something different. Except I fucking love what I did!” He erupts into guffaws. “I work really hard on my shows, and I genuinely love them. I think there are waves of hatred, and maybe in a few years it’ll be more appreciated. But it’s appreciated by ME!” What does he think it would take to save the show? “Part of the problem is that there seem to be spasms and ruptures and cuts at the BBC. My worry is that there’s nobody there to champion it. You need a producer saying: ‘What about Doctor Who? What about Doctor Who? What about Doctor Who?’ every single day. That’s gone. In 2005, I made it exactly like a 9pm ITV drama, with a lot of the rhythms of everyday life. That concept has gone now, so maybe it’ll end up as a vertical drama [clip shows designed to be watched on a smartphone] with a cliffhanger every two minutes? When it returns, it should be part of whatever the rest of telly is doing.” He won’t be drawn on who he should be the next Doctor. “I’ve made the mistake of saying so-and-so would be good, and the next thing you know, journalists are at their door.”

For now, Davies remains a free agent, and you’d be naive to try to predict his next move. After the success of Queer As Folk he immediately alienated a sub-sector of his gay audience by making a romcom, Bob and Rose, in which a gay man falls in love with a woman; when It’s a Sin broke streaming records, he followed it with the not-exactly-timely miniseries about Noele Gordon’s sacking from Crossroads in 1981. In 2015, when the head of BBC drama commissioning paid him a home visit following the ratings hit of his first four series of Doctor Who, Davies leveraged their interest to make his version of A Midsummer Night’s Dream, starring Elaine Paige. He spoke to Harvey Weinstein about providing extra financing, but got the creeps. “I should have been running after the money, he could’ve solved all our problems, but I couldn’t even bear a phone call with the man. He was just baleful, he gave me the shivers. My producer Faith Penhale, who was on the call, might as well not have been. She had the schedules, the budgets – and he just dismissed her.”

While his pedigree now affords him a degree of creative freedom, Christmas 2017 found Davies in a position where the BBC had initially turned down Years and Years, while It’s a Sin had originally been rejected by the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 (one executive asked if Davies knew Elton John and suggested that he might be able to turn it into a musical). He says he’s fond of a Tolstoy quote: “The revolutions have to keep on happening.” Only, “I looked it up the other day and there’s no record of him saying that, so maybe I made it up!” Does he feel that he kicks doors open, only to watch them close again? “You know those slow pneumatic hinges that close automatically? I think that’s what happens. They ‘hisss’ closed slowly.”

His ideas gestate for years – decades even – before they’re committed to the page in a flurry (he first had the idea for It’s a Sin more than 30 years ago; one Doctor Who script was written in the course of a weekend). Unusually, his first draft is often his final draft. Bonham Carter has said of Nolly that: “It’s the only time I’ve ever been involved in something that the script that I read ended up immaculately on the screen. There was not one thing cut, not one thing re-ordered.” Davies recently struck upon a fresh idea, and sent the first script to his producer, only for her to remind him that he’d already pitched it to her back in 2018. After the operatic trauma of Tip Toe, he’s hoping to give this one a happy ending. “I’m very excited. These are strange days for telly, so I hope it gets made.” And if not? “I’ll write something else.” The revolutions will keep happening.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘My hips can’t help but move’: readers on the songs that always get them dancing
EntertainmentTab.text:
I Don’t Feel Like Dancin’ – Scissor Sisters

My now-husband and I attended a wedding. The reception was boring. No one was dancing and people were wondering if it was too early to leave. We sat at our table thinking what song would get everyone up on to the dancefloor. We chose I Don’t Feel Like Dancin’. When I asked the DJ to play it he laughed and said: “That’s appropriate.” We danced by ourselves and people started joining us. The party kicked off and we all had a great time. Years later, we played the song at our own wedding. It makes me happy. Rachael, 46, Warrington

Celebrity Skin – Hole

I used to go to rock clubs in the early 2000s and this was the only song they’d play with a female vocalist. Me and my friend danced like maniacs, forcing the guys off the dancefloor. Heather, London

Return of the Mack – Mark Morrison

It’s a guilty pleasure for sure, but Return of the Mack always gets me out there. It has been a favourite of mine and my twin brother’s since we first heard it. The melody transcends the cheese and lyrics to make it a booty bopper I can’t resist. The last time my brother and I were back home at a very stodgy bar, this surprisingly came on and we immediately transformed the bar into our dancefloor. Some others actually followed. Music truly does transcend all. Dave, 56, Portland, US

I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor – Arctic Monkeys

It’s a song that I’ve grown up with and was a staple at the nightclub Welly in Hull that I used to go to when I was in sixth form and university. It was the first song I put down when my wife and I were choosing our wedding evening playlist. It’s timeless. Chris Brough, 31, York

Temptation – New Order

An extremely danceable classic from an iconic band, which is guaranteed to get everybody up and moving. Calle Jershed, 55, Gothenburg, Sweden

Rock Lobster – The B-52s

This is the one that always gets me up, wherever I am. It’s like I was hypnotised way back when I first heard it – I always immediately spring up from my seat when it’s on. Julie Gibson, 61, Northamptonshire

I Believe in Miracles – The Jackson Sisters

It’s soulful, funky and utterly hypnotic – the song grabs me instantly. Bernd Wagner, Mainz, Germany

Groove Is in the Heart – Deee-Lite

It is still sensational, and so inventive. It pops and crackles along at a rollicking pace, Lady Miss Kier’s vocals give way to insane drum breaks, and it never grows old. It’s funky as hell and just wonderful. Alex, 52, Southampton

Last Dance – Donna Summer

When I was a college student in the 70s, I loved going to discos. This is such a joyful song. To this day, when I hear it I cannot sit still. Terry Heimbaugh, 70, Illinois, US

Sex & Drugs & Rock & Roll – Ian Dury

Opening with an ambitious drum roll, it moves instantly into a killer riff. This song combines whimsical lyrics with tightly executed funk that’s an absolute joy to dance to. Kate, East Cambridgeshire

Blinding Lights – The Weeknd

My taste is eclectic, but rarely includes songs that chart. This is a gorgeous exception. The composition is so simple but it’s combined into something so full and rich. Immediately I’m dancing. Jack, 32, Bristol

Man 2 Man Meets Man Parrish – Male Stripper

This song will always get me on the dancefloor. It’s so catchy and the opening few bars are so distinctive that it puts a massive smile on my face. Tim, 60, Prestwick

Butter has a great beat and has also helped me introduce more people to the world of K-pop. It holds great memories for me, of connecting to other people when I was feeling low. This song just has a way of bringing people together, no matter what genre they like. Gwen, Sydney, Australia

Rocks – Primal Scream

Yes, it’s a Rolling Stones rip-off but it is pure adrenaline and rock’n’roll euphoria. Dave Ross,Glasgow

California Love – 2Pac ft Dr Dre

As soon as I hear those first few notes, my hips can’t help but move. 2Pac’s “shake it, shake it, baby” is a command I cannot deny. Something about this song reminds me of being 18, hitting the dancefloor and being carefree. Rachael, 39, Sydney, Australia

Do I Love You (Indeed I Do) – Frank Wilson

I have always loved Northern soul and Do I Love You (Indeed I Do) is the song which always gets me dancing. I will often request it at wedding functions. It brings back memories of a bygone age, growing up in a deprived area where music was a way of gathering together at the local youth club. Julie, 68, Shropshire

Brimful of Asha – Cornershop

When I hear it, I absolutely can’t stay still, no matter how knackered I am. And I can listen to it time after time and not get sick of it. Barbara Manighetti, 65, Wellington, New Zealand

Move on Up – Curtis Mayfield

It’s the greatest song ever written in my opinion – it has just four main chords, but it’s so uplifting. Michael, 43, Madrid, Spain

Jump Around – House of Pain

The distinctive horn at the beginning is like a calling, and then the hip-hop beat starts, and you’re already a goner within the first few seconds. There’s something about the track: not only do you jump, but you also want to shout out the chorus on the dancefloor. It’s a 90s banger with attitude. Sofia Ilyas, 45, London

Ice Ice Baby – Vanilla Ice

I remember my two sisters and I dancing to this song when it played on MTV back in the 90s. We would jump around the living room. I still listen to it now, dancing around the house with my dogs watching curiously. It triggers a happiness switch in my mind. Lara, 39, Bengaluru, India

Let Me Be Your Fantasy – Baby D

I only have to hear the whisper of “Let me be your fantasy” at the beginning and I’ll be on the floor dragging anyone in my path. This track is such a mood booster. Debbie, 51, London

Mr Brightside – The Killers

It was once played at a friend’s wedding – I maniacally jumped up and down on the dancefloor and the bride audibly guffawed. Neil Vicker, 63, Newbury

GeneralTab.title: Burnham scraps controversial plans to curb jury trials
GeneralTab.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has scrapped controversial plans to curb some jury trials.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had introduced proposals to allow judges to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-alone - and it proposes that thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he had changed course after hearing the "strength of feeling" about the original proposals.

Criminal lawyers have welcomed the decision and the Conservatives say it is a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury.

Former Justice Secretary David Lammy first announced the plans in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases - having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during the national lockdowns. Official projections have estimated it could reach 100,000 before the next general election and, in a worst case scenario, climb to double that number by 2035.

There are, however, indications the backlog is now stabilising after the government committed unlimited funding to pay for more judges to sit in courts that were otherwise being unused.

Under the original plans, Lammy had wanted to reserve jury trials for the most serious "indictable" offences - meaning cases that are always sent to Crown Court, including murder and rape.

Less serious offences, where the sentence would be no more than three years, would be decided without a jury in the Crown Court by a judge alone. Even less serious offences would stay in magistrates' courts, abolishing defendants' right to ask for a trial by jury when they feel that is their best chance of beig cleared.

The proposals triggered an outcry across many parts of the criminal justice world, with many opponents saying that eroding the 800-year-old right to trial by jury would not solve the backlogs.

GeneralTab.title: Conservatives pledge to scrap £100,000 childcare 'cliff edge'
GeneralTab.text:
The Conservatives have promised to scrap the "absurd cliff edge" that mean parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Under the current system, only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for government-funded or tax-free childcare.

"What we want to see is that people who work harder don't get punished for doing so," Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham.

The party said the move would be a "first step" in broader efforts to address issues in the tax system which damage incentives to work or invest.

This will be a theme of shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith's conference speech on Monday.

Since September 2025, working parents in England have been entitled to 30 hours of free childcare, external for children aged between nine months and four years old.

However, to qualify both parents must earn less than £100,000 a year.

The same £100,000 threshold applies to the government's tax-free childcare scheme, external.

For every £8 paid into an online childcare account, the government adds £2, up to £2,000 per child per year, which parents can then use to pay for childcare.

The Tories said that if they return to power they would remove the £100,000 threshold entirely so parents no longer lose childcare support when their income exceeds this level.

GeneralTab.title: Ex-City trader How to spot a psychopath at work
GeneralTab.text:
Most of us have had colleagues who can be tricky to work with.

They may act impulsively, be manipulative, or even outright lie to advance their careers - but how can you tell the difference between an unpleasant co-worker and someone displaying psychopathic traits?

Geraint Anderson, a former London banker-turned author, said he was assessed by a clinical psychologist who told him he may have had "situational psychopathy" in order to succeed in the cut-throat corporate world.

"I had to really become a kind of worse version of myself in order to thrive in this environment," he said.

Anderson, 53, who now lives in Monmouthshire, said some modern workplaces and social influences reward psychopathic traits.

He worked for 12 years as an analyst in London's financial district and earned millions of pounds before leaving his job ahead of the financial crash in 2008.

"The city rewards this dark triad behaviour... being uber confident, being able to control and manipulate others, not getting emotionally involved in decisions and being decisive," he said.

"I adapted myself for the city and started bringing out the kind of worst side of myself."

A psychopath is someone with an antisocial personality disorder, external, rather than a clinical diagnosis itself.

People with these disorders think and act differently to others and, among other things:

Exploit or manipulate others

Lack regret or remorse

Behave irresponsibly

Have difficulty sustaining long-term relationships

Are unable to control their anger

Lack guilt and blame others for problems in their lives

In his early 20s, Anderson was enjoying life in Goa, India, selling trinkets to tourists on the beach.

His brother convinced him to apply for a finance job, which he only intended to do for a few years.

"I cut off my ponytail, shaved off my beard, took all my earrings out, bought a £60 suit - all that's totally true - the day before I had my interview."

Once he had his foot in the door as an intern, success became an obsession, with bonuses becoming "a way of gauging how wonderfully successful a human being I was".

This figure allowed him to compare himself to people at other banks and "really appealed to my competitiveness".

He believes some of the traits that helped him climb the ranks were those associated with psychopathy.

"I had a degree of fearlessness. I had a bit of - dare I say - glib charm. I wasn't hugely emotionally affected by things that happened on the trading floor."

Anderson said a lot of traits psychopaths possess are ones "that the corporate environment rewards" and are "incredibly useful in high-powered jobs in the city".

He added the most important thing when it comes to psychopaths is "you don't promote them, you don't marry them and you don't vote for them."

Robert Snowden, a Cardiff University psychologist, has studied psychopathy for about 25 years and has worked with Robert Hare, the creator of the psychopathy checklist (PCL-R).

It consists of 20 questions, each scoring between zero and two, with a maximum score of 40.

Snowden said most people scored below five, while 25 or over was typically the threshold for psychopathy.

Anderson scored himself about an eight or a nine.

"Psychopathy is on a dimension that I could place you, I could place myself," Snowden said.

Despite rapidly rising through the ranks of London finance, Anderson said he became disillusioned by "greed, reckless risk-taking and rule breaking in the industry".

"I just looked around and thought 'I'm on the wrong team'... What on Earth are you doing? You are part of the problem."

He left and became the anonymous columnist City Boy, for the London Paper every Friday, revealing a world of excessive wining, dining, drugs and illicit sex.

It transformed into a the book Cityboy that sold more than 400,000 copies and was translated into six languages.

He's also recently just published his fifth book which explores how adopting psychopathic traits can help people climb the corporate ladder.

Anderson said he was a "less pleasant person" while in the corporate world but hopes he is a "warmer person" now

"I'm more able to feel like trying to have integrity and not manipulate and be ruthless."

Although, he joked, his wife may disagree about him not having any of his psychopathic traits left.

GeneralTab.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
GeneralTab.text:
The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket.

It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement.

The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months.

Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports, there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members.

The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.

Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.

On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."

His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.

Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".

Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing."

"Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said.

"And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do."

Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies.

Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.

Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".

Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".

In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."

It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.

The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.

European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.

The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.

articles.title: Burnham scraps controversial plans to curb jury trials
articles.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has scrapped controversial plans to curb some jury trials.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had introduced proposals to allow judges to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-alone - and it proposes that thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said he had changed course after hearing the "strength of feeling" about the original proposals.

Criminal lawyers have welcomed the decision and the Conservatives say it is a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury.

Former Justice Secretary David Lammy first announced the plans in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases - having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during the national lockdowns. Official projections have estimated it could reach 100,000 before the next general election and, in a worst case scenario, climb to double that number by 2035.

There are, however, indications the backlog is now stabilising after the government committed unlimited funding to pay for more judges to sit in courts that were otherwise being unused.

Under the original plans, Lammy had wanted to reserve jury trials for the most serious "indictable" offences - meaning cases that are always sent to Crown Court, including murder and rape.

Less serious offences, where the sentence would be no more than three years, would be decided without a jury in the Crown Court by a judge alone. Even less serious offences would stay in magistrates' courts, abolishing defendants' right to ask for a trial by jury when they feel that is their best chance of beig cleared.

The proposals triggered an outcry across many parts of the criminal justice world, with many opponents saying that eroding the 800-year-old right to trial by jury would not solve the backlogs.

articles.title: Conservatives pledge to scrap £100,000 childcare 'cliff edge'
articles.text:
The Conservatives have promised to scrap the "absurd cliff edge" that mean parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.

Under the current system, only families where no parent earns more than this threshold are eligible for government-funded or tax-free childcare.

"What we want to see is that people who work harder don't get punished for doing so," Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.

The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham.

The party said the move would be a "first step" in broader efforts to address issues in the tax system which damage incentives to work or invest.

This will be a theme of shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith's conference speech on Monday.

Since September 2025, working parents in England have been entitled to 30 hours of free childcare, external for children aged between nine months and four years old.

However, to qualify both parents must earn less than £100,000 a year.

The same £100,000 threshold applies to the government's tax-free childcare scheme, external.

For every £8 paid into an online childcare account, the government adds £2, up to £2,000 per child per year, which parents can then use to pay for childcare.

The Tories said that if they return to power they would remove the £100,000 threshold entirely so parents no longer lose childcare support when their income exceeds this level.

The threshold has been criticised by economists, who point out it can leave parents worse off overall even after a pay rise of tens of thousands of pounds.

Badenoch told the BBC the party didn't want "people to stop working because of that".

Speaking before the party's conference, she added: "What we want to see is more people in work and not taking the wrong decisions or the wrong choices, and it doesn't matter whether they're earning £10,000 or £100,000 - what matters is that people are out there working".

Asked if this could result in someone who earns £1 million a year get free childcare under a Conservative government, Badenoch responded: "It doesn't matter what you earn - we don't want you to be punished for working hard. What we're trying to do is grow our economy."

articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
articles.text:
The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.

The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.

Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.

Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

A crash axe is usually kept ​in the cockpit in case of emergencies.

The weapon used has been a key question for investigators, given the stringent security on such a sensitive route. Early reports from passengers on board had suggested it might have been a knife.

The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.

The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times have named him as Hamam al-Hammami. There has been no official confirmation of this.

While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.

He completed a three-year distance-learning course at Buckinghamshire New University in the UK and graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said that after the attacker was subdued on the flight, he called out to the crew "Kill me, kill me!"

The Israeli prime minister added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."

He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".

The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.

He also said investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.

Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.

The pilot, who is from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.

"I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said.

articles.title: Man shot dead in East Acton as people gather for memorial service
articles.text:
A murder investigation has been launched after a 40-year-old man was shot dead in a "senseless act of violence" as up to 50 people – including children – gathered for a memorial service in west London.

The Met Police said it was called to the scene at 19:47 GMT on Friday after multiple shots had been heard by members of the public at the junction of Braybrook Street and Erconwald Street in East Acton.

Officers attended alongside the London Ambulance Service but the man was pronounced dead at the scene, despite the efforts of medics.

No arrests have been made and a police cordon remains in place in Braybrook Street. Police are appealing for witnesses to come forward.

The victim's family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.

A post-mortem examination is scheduled to establish the cause of death, but the victim is believed to have sustained a gunshot wound, the force said.

Det Ch Insp Brian Howie, who is leading the investigation, said: "Our thoughts are with the family and friends of a man whose life was taken in a senseless act of violence.

"We understand a large number of people had gathered for a memorial service and what should have been a time to come together in remembrance has instead left a family devastated.

"We believe between 40 and 50 people, including children, were present when this incident occurred. Someone knows what happened and we need them to come forward."

He has asked anyone who was around Erconwald Street, Braybrook Street, the surrounding roads or Wormwood Scrubs playground between 18:00 and 20:00, to "please think carefully about what you saw".

He added: "Did you see anyone carrying or concealing weapons, people on bicycles acting suspiciously, or vehicles being driven at speed?

"We also want to hear from anyone with photographs, video, dashcam, doorbell or mobile phone footage or who has seen anything relevant on social media.

"However insignificant it may seem, the smallest piece of information could prove crucial in helping us establish what happened and identify those responsible."

articles.title: When parenting advice becomes too much
articles.text:
Before Rosie Whitfield became a mum, she imagined herself parenting very calm children.

"Then I had two wild boys," she says with a laugh.

Following the birth of her kids, Rosie spent hours online looking for the best advice and was drawn to one particular approach to parenting: Gentle parenting, which focuses on empathy and mutual respect with little emphasis on punishment, albeit with boundaries.

But she constantly worried her choices, from sleep schedules to handling toddler tantrums, were "ruining their lives forever".

Rosie does not blame the gentle parenting philosophy itself but instead says the overall amount of parenting advice online was "overwhelming" and "made mundane parenting choices feel like the absolute end of the world."

"I felt like if I was choosing to put the TV on for 20 minutes while I did the dishes or had a coffee, I was choosing to destroy my children's brains," says Rosie, who is originally from Birmingham and now lives in Dubai.

Rosie believes her confidence and intuition were stripped away as she questioned every parenting decision. And she is not alone.

Government research suggests that around two-thirds of parents with young children feel overwhelmed by the amount of parenting information available and struggle with conflicting advice, with many turning to social media for support.

And it's not just the early years.

Research from the charity Action for Children found that many parents of teenagers who initially contacted the charity for help with school avoidance, ADHD or mental health, often went on to describe their own anxiety, exhaustion and uncertainty of how to parent with empathy and patience when close to burnout.

Faced with an array of parenting philosophies, or "brands" to choose from, is all of this advice helping parents or making them more anxious? And is there really a best way to parent? Or, as we strive to become the perfect parent, are we losing our intuition?

Parents today are confronted by parenting styles including "helicopter parenting", which is focused on closely monitoring and protecting children from harm, and "tiger parenting", which involves strict parenting and high expectations for achievement. There are also "snowplough parents", who try to remove obstacles from their child's path, and "dolphin parents", who aim to be firm but flexible.

Author Matilda Gosling, who wrote Evidence‑Based Parenting, says many of the parenting fads or trends complicate what should be a straightforward relationship between a parent and child.

"Some parents think 'I need to be a snowplough parent and plough all of these obstacles out of the way'."

"But it really complicates what is actually a fairly fundamental part of being human, which is that you are warm and you love your children and you put in place some boundaries around them."

One of the most widely studied models of parenting comes from developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind.

Baumrind identified three parenting styles, later expanded to four: authoritative (high warmth and high control), authoritarian (low warmth and high control), permissive (high warmth and low control), and neglectful (low warmth and low control).

"Authoritative is the gold standard," says Gosling who has looked at more than 1,000 studies.

Research has found that children raised with an authoritative approach, combining warmth with clear boundaries, tend to achieve better academic results, have higher self-esteem and stronger social skills.

But where gentle parenting fits within that framework is disputed. Gosling believes that it falls on the permissive side.

"It's very much child-led. The child ends up having so much control that there's no sense of safety coming from the outside."

However, Sarah Ockwell-Smith, who is widely credited with coining and popularising the term 'gentle parenting', strongly disagrees.

"It [gentle parenting] is not remotely permissive," she says, putting it firmly in Baumrind's authoritative category. Clear boundaries are "super important".

Social media, however, is flooded with memes of exhausted parents calmly negotiating with a child having a supermarket meltdown, something Ockwell-Smith finds deeply frustrating.

"I have to step away from the Instagram reels and the TikToks because I just want to comment, 'This is not gentle parenting'".

"You have house rules, family limits, discipline and consequences. But the difference is we look at discipline as learning and teaching rather than punishing."

Toddler tantrums and teenage behaviour, she argues, should be viewed through a lens of ongoing brain development, not 'they're being naughty' or 'they hate me'.

But despite the term being popular, Ockwell-Smith believes that gentle parenting is still a fringe movement and that authoritarian parenting remains the dominant style.

Around 80 years ago, American paediatrician Dr Benjamin Spock published a book called Baby and Child Care, which went on to sell millions of copies and became the main source of advice for mothers for generations.

The opening line was "Trust yourself. You know more than you think..."

The book challenged strict parenting norms of the time and in the following decades parents were offered more advice from an increasing range of voices.

Research into parenting has increasingly focused on the early years - from pregnancy to the age of two when the building blocks for lifelong emotional and physical health are laid down. For parents, that means more advice to navigate competing messages about what is best for their children.

Professor Ellie Lee, the director of the Centre for Parenting Culture Studies, has studied parenting for more than two decades, including research into mothers' confidence and uncertainty around infant feeding.

She says a major shift occurred in the 1990s when parenting became an increasing focus of public policy.

"Politicians started to say 'Parenting's the hardest job in the world. Children don't come with a manual. We need to give parents guidance. Parents need more support. We need parent education'."

Advice began to emerge on almost every aspect of family life, from tummy time, to feeding, to the right buggy, she explains.

Prof Lee argues that while some public health campaigns were necessary, such as advice not to put babies to sleep on their front after research into cot deaths, the growing culture of advice began to make parents paranoid.

"Dr Spock's 'trust yourself' philosophy is now a very counter-cultural piece of advice," she says. "What we say instead is 'always seek help',"

She believes this has made parents more anxious about doing things "right".

"Some of the things that are now presented as really high stakes are not," she says, using examples like breastfeeding exclusively for six months or how much tummy time a child needs.

"It's terrible because parents become completely exhausted."

Ockwell-Smith says the volume of advice can be "deafening and confusing".

"Actually, parents should just learn themselves and go on intuition," she says.

Others point out that there is also a problem of advice being given that is altogether wrong. Ruth Watts is a health visitor who began sharing content on social media after becoming concerned about misinformation online.

She had seen "experts" advise parents to wean babies onto solids early, offer treatment advice for tongue tie or allergies without medical training, and tell parents to put babies in their own rooms before six months.

Many families, she argues, are working longer hours while at the same time health services are being stripped back, leaving more parents looking online for breastfeeding, behaviour and sleep support.

"We are looking for that kind of personable, conversational approach from people, rather than reading a website."

Many factors shaping family life remain outside parents' control. A child's temperament, special educational needs, family support, finances and their own upbringing can all influence family life.

While some say parenting hasn't got harder but expectations have, others argue that parents today are facing more complex challenges than in previous generations with growing concerns around young people's mental health.

There are also debates around children spending more time on screens and less time outdoors, while schools are reporting increasing behavioural challenges and lower respect for rules and authority. Prof Lee believes parental confidence is at an all-time low.

"I think parents feel very nervous about disciplining children now because they're worried about how it's going to make them feel," she argues.

The confusion around the "right" way to parent has led some parents to turn to courses for help.

Aymara Lamche-Brennan, who has a 22-year-old daughter, four-year-old son and six-month-old daughter, signed up for a course during the summer when another mother at the school gate mentioned she was attending.

"The flyer said 'it's the toughest job in the world' and I thought yes it is, how can you help?'" Aymara says from her home in London.

"When I had my daughter, I was 19 and I didn't really think much about parenting styles, she was with me everywhere and I just kind of rolled with it, but what I really want to know now is what simple wins are there with parenting?"

Aymara said the Circle of Security course she attended gave her practical tools so she could help her children organise their feelings, take charge when she needs to and recognise when she was becoming stressed.

"It's not telling you how to parent. It's helping you think," says Jennifer Peters, a former social worker and director of the charity Connected Lives which runs courses across London, Derbyshire and Cambridgeshire.

She says most parents want the best for their kids but they don't always know how to get there, and that guidance can be helpful.

"I don't think people need to be bombarded with information but the group experience helps you think, 'oh, it's not just me' and lets you take a step back from it all," Peters says.

Back in Dubai, Rosie says the arrival of her second child changed everything as she realised her sons were "polar opposites" and there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

A recent trip home to Birmingham also provided some perspective. Her eldest son was throwing a tantrum, and Rosie found herself wrestling with a familiar worry.

"If I send him upstairs, am I damaging him emotionally? Is he going to develop an attachment disorder because of this?"

But her mum said, 'Just send him upstairs. He can't hit his brother over the head with a horse [if he is upstairs]. Follow through with your actions.'

Rosie is taking this "generational advice" on board and has started "venting on social media" to show other mums that they are not alone.

Looking back on her first few years of being a mum, she said she wished she had known one thing.

"There isn't the perfect parent."

articles.title: Why Canada is preparing for a (longshot) US invasion
articles.text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.

Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.

"That's just risk management," Carney said.

Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.

In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.

"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.

Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.

But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.

In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.

A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.

"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.

Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.

They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.

The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.

Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.

After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.

But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.

"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.

Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.

Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.

In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.

Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.

Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.

It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.

They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.

A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.

"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."

Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.

He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.

"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.

Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.

So what would it be like if it happened?

The first phase of a war could be quite short.

According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week

Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.

Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.

The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.

The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.

He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.

An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.

Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.

"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.

"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."

Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.

But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.

"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.

Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

articles.title: Laura Kuenssberg: Kemi Badenoch has cemented her image. Now she wants to take her party back to its roots
articles.text:
The 2026 Conservative conference is big enough to justify using Birmingham's Symphony Hall as its main stage again.

So, Kemi Badenoch will tread the same stage ageing rockers Marillion took last month - and where sequinned soprano Katherine Jenkins will perform next week. She'll also avoid the humiliation of a national party leader being squashed into a side room at a corporate conference centre (with drapes portioning off the empty space). Simply, the party is able to put bums on seats again - and by that measure, things are looking up.

Badenoch goes into the conference with her own position secure in the party. One senior Tory says "she has actually defied cynics like me" who initially disapproved of her leadership. Her standing with the public has improved and she is now, again on a very simple but crucial measure, much better known. Her allies are sure she has developed a clear identity among the public, confiding: "People now know who she is and they enjoy her interventions - the thing we hear most is I don't always agree with her but I know where she stands."

But Conservative MPs are aware that the party itself still has a much bigger issue - in the words of one shadow cabinet member: "The problem we still have is trust of the party and the brand". The shadow of the years of chaos still looms. And while Badenoch has made good progress since she took the job, most of that was up against an unpopular prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, on whom she landed plenty of political punches. She has to show "what being Conservative is now", says another senior Tory, taking on a different, more popular, rival in Andy Burnham.

The Tories' warm-up to conference has been so far, so traditional. A proposed dramatic expansion of prison places kicks off Badenoch's second big party get-together. With it, a message that echoes the well-known mantra of the early 1990s Tories, issued by former leader Michael Howard at party conference: "Prison works". They are not just talking about adding on a few cells here and there, but spelling out a monumental increase in the numbers of people that the country locks up.

That follows the announcement of a new "tough love" approach for young people trying to claim benefits. Don't expect the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whateley, to produce a moment as controversial as when the then-welfare secretary, Peter Lilley, proclaimed from the stage that he had "a little list" of benefit claimants he wanted to root out. But the Conservatives are determined to keep concentrating on the size of the welfare bill – believing it's right to do so for financial and moral reasons.

You can expect to hear more in the week about fundamental conservative principles: people keeping more of their own money, government only stepping in when really required to, pointed concern about the level of the country's debt and public spending. And again, of course, that means Kemi Badenoch disavowing much of what the Conservatives did in office between 2010 and 2024, when the civil service grew, the tax burden grew, a law was passed to try to combat climate change, the list goes on.

She'll set out at some length in the coming days what she sees as classic conservative first principles: the core beliefs the party was founded on and drifted from, she reckons, in the years gone by. If anything, Badenoch told interviewers this week the party was "finally saying what we believe" and "should be more aggressive" in displaying the party's core.

She believes the arrival of Andy Burnham makes that easier. There's a clearer contrast between the two. A senior ally of Badenoch says Burnham has "opened the door to it quite well, as he has harked back to the '70s in a way that I'm astonished by". Suggesting the pleasing atmospherics of Burnham's Labour are just that, atmospherics, the ally adds: "It's like a fairy story where he has come to the rescue of Britain and he has a wand in his hand and nothing else".

As we talked about a couple of weeks ago, the contrasts between Labour and the Conservatives are sharper now Burnham is in post, and the conference season is only serving to exaggerate that. They are both only too happy to emphasise it with their messages, retro or not, designed to show the true souls of their tribes.

But while Badenoch might find it easier to argue clearly with Burnham, rather than tangle with Starmer over process, it is harder to face an opponent who, at least for now, is proving more appealing to the public. And while plenty of Conservatives are hopeful in private that Reform might have peaked, they can't be sure that's true, or that the swathes of voters who abandoned the Tories for Farage's party will return.

Badenoch has always seemed allergic to the idea of doing any kind of deal with Reform, who she dismisses as a party of protest. And her allies hope, and some believe, that Reform's appeal will fade, making the Conservatives again the obvious alternative government. But fundamental arithmetic displays that, for as long as millions of voters on the right are tempted by Farage, it's harder for the Tories to triumph. One shadow minister admits "we've still got a whole battle on the right" even though "Kemi's boldness" is beginning to break through.

So, in the coming next days, prepare for a "classic showing of Tory wares": an attempt by the party's leader to set out their fundamental beliefs about the country and how it should be governed.

There are pockets of nerves that Kemi Badenoch risks rewinding to an previous era. One when another newly confident leader, David Cameron, ushered in the modern Tory party on the conference stage in front of digitally produced green foliage and sunlight. One former cabinet minister warns that it's "the big risk – so easy to slip into an alienating divisive manner – nasty party stuff".

When it comes to policy, and striking the right tone, they warn that Badenoch must "be mindful that she has to win Cheltenham and Maidenhead as well as Clacton".

But Kemi Badenoch is visibly more confident and is aware of the chance in front of her – seemingly unworried about the possible downsides of making an increasingly direct argument to you, eager to stride that mercifully bigger Birmingham stage.

articles.title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
articles.text:
Tens of thousands of people have protested across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation.

About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona.

"There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.

The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.

Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.

Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.

His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.

One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000.

Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city".

Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.

One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."

Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros.

Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid".

Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square.

On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".

It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.

The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.

House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.

The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.

It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

articles.title: 'Another tax bombshell?' and 'Terror plot targets'
articles.text:
Andy Burnham's latest plans feature in several of today's papers. The Sunday Express asks readers whether "Another tax bombshell?" will fund Burnham's social care revolution. Experts warn that workers could face another tax rise since the PM's "controversial sacrifice of the pension triple lock" will not fully cover the cost of his social care plan, the paper reports.

The Observer splashes on Andy Burnham's "road back from Brexit" alongside an image of the prime minister with the stars from the EU flag apparently reflected in his glasses. The Observer's view is that the potential opening back to Europe "has the potential to be historic" for the leader and for Britain.

In a move described as "yet another reversal of one of Sir Keir Starmer's flagship policies", Andy Burnham has scrapped controversial plans to cut thousands of jury trials across England and Wales, according to the Independent.

The court appearance of two Iranian men harged with "plotting terror attacks at key Jewish sites" in Manchester makes the front page of the Sunday Mirror. The paper shows a synagogue and museum as two of the alleged targets.

The Sunday Telegraph has more revelations about the co-pilot accused of attacking his fellow pilot on a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel earlier this week. Under the headline "Hijacker's hate rants while at UK university", the paper outlines claims about his time on a distance-learning course at Buckinghamshire New University. It said the pilot "advocated violence against women" and "called for severe religious punishments" in posts on Twitter, during the time he was completing the course as a remote student between 2020 and 2023.

Former heavyweight champion Tyson Fury has said he wants US President Donald Trump to lead him to the ring "for his epic showdown with Anthony Joshua", according to the Daily Star. Fury and AJ are set to meet in an all-British bout at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

Sir Kevin Sinfield is in a "league of his own", the Sunday People reports, after he completed his latest endurance challenge to raise money for motor neurone disease causes in memory of his friend and team-mate Rob Burrow, who died in 2024. Meanwhile, the paper headlines on parents of a murdered teen who want to "silence cruel web 'sleuths'."

A Mail on Sunday exclusive reveals small boat migrants have received more than 1,000 free hijabs this year. According to internal government figures the UK has handed out 162 hijabs a month to migrants arriving by boat, the paper says.

The Sun on Sunday leads with former England striker Andy Carroll confirming he was sexually assaulted "by a star of BBC show Fame Academy". Carroll first revealed he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021 in an autobiography titled 'Owning it', which came out in September. Dance coach Kevin Adams was convicted in 2023 and jailed, the paper reports.

And the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) was given "preferential access" to property developments in Manchester under a "sweetheart deal" with the city council, according to the Sunday Times. ADUG owns Manchester City Football Club, the paper says.
